items.headline: Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online outage lasted about 24 hours; Microsoft cites gateway software bug
items.summary: Exchange Online and Outlook were unreachable for many customers worldwide from 16:20 GMT on 12 November to 16:10 on 13 November. Microsoft's preliminary report blames a latent gateway bug, not an attack; its final report is due 20 November.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Microsoft published a preliminary report; CEO Nadella and multiple outlets confirmed the bug. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: Thursday 12 November 2026, 16:20 GMT, Microsoft Service Health notice EX1550543 (per Microsoft's preliminary report)

sections.happened: Most users could not reach Exchange Online mailboxes via Outlook or other clients from 16:20 GMT on 12 November, and email was delayed for many. Microsoft tracked it as EX1550543 and MO1550821; Copilot, Teams calendars, Defender and Purview features that use Exchange were also affected. Impact ended at 16:10 GMT on 13 November. Microsoft said it was not a cyberattack. CEO Satya Nadella called it a "perfect storm" and said testing should have caught it.
sections.technical: Microsoft's preliminary report (15 November) names three factors. A July fix to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers contained a lock-contention defect, missed because test labs used older hardware with fewer cores. Teams traffic failed over to the shared primary gateway about fifteen hours earlier. Nearly 14% of capacity was already out of service. Over 80% of servers stopped responding at the lowest point. Recovered servers were re-overwhelmed; a revert update began at 07:20 GMT on 13 November.
sections.guidance: Microsoft said tenants need not change anything. It extended the email delivery window so delayed messages were not returned as undeliverable. It lists added capacity, extra traffic-redirection monitoring and traffic-distribution guardrails as completed repairs; a full repair list is planned for 20 November.
sections.differing: Commentators speculated about attacks or AI agents; Microsoft and US officials found no sign of either. Nadella linked such incidents partly to faster AI-driven patching, which is his view, not a finding in Microsoft's report.
sections.unknown: Final root-cause report and full repair items are pending. Exact numbers of affected tenants and users have not been published by Microsoft.

sources.title: 365Fanatic: summary and PDF of Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report, 15 Nov 2026

items.headline: Apple services (App Store, Music, iCloud, AppleCare) briefly disrupted in US on 17 November
items.summary: Apple's status page showed problems with App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare and some iCloud services on Tuesday 17 November. Apple said users faced a problem it was resolving; cause unpublished. A reported NSA network outage the same day is linked only by timing.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.labelBasis: Apple acknowledged a service problem; no cause or scale published. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: About 18:00 UK, 17 Nov 2026 (NBC Chicago, quoting Apple statement just before noon CT)

sections.happened: On Tuesday 17 November 2026 Apple's system status page showed problems affecting Apple Music, AppleCare, some iCloud services and the App Store, NBC Chicago reported. Apple told NBC News: "Users are experiencing a problem with this service. We are working to resolve this issue." Staff at Apple's Michigan Avenue store in Chicago said their system was down for at least an hour; it appeared operational by 12:20 p.m. CT (18:20 UK). Downdetector, cited by Forbes Middle East, logged more than 2,300 Apple Pay and 1,800 iCloud reports.
sections.differing: A BNN Bloomberg video headline carried by CTV says Apple blamed the outage on an 'internal update'; the text read did not confirm this. Officials said the wider run of US outages was not a cyber-attack; Apple has not published a cause.
sections.unknown: Apple's root cause, exact start and end times, and affected regions are unpublished. Any link to the separate reported NSA network disruption is unestablished; officials described that as maintenance.

items.headline: Equinor cyberattack hits IT systems; oil and gas output unaffected
items.summary: Norwegian energy major Equinor says an ongoing cyber-attack targets certain IT systems. Production runs normally and there is no indication data was stolen. Attackers are unidentified.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.labelBasis: Company statements and press reports; attacker, vector and scope undisclosed.
items.firstReported: 17 Nov 2026, 17:55 UK time (18:55 CET), Equinor statement on equinor.com

sections.happened: Equinor said on 17 November it had detected an ongoing cyber-attack on certain IT systems. Updates on 18 and 19 November said the attack continues, does not appear to target Equinor specifically, and has not affected production. Reuters reported internal email was down; staff may struggle with some corporate applications. Police informed.
sections.technical: Vector, actor and affected systems not disclosed. Equinor says it is 'not a virus attack', so no self-spreading risk. No attributed group; Norway's NSM raised national cyber risk to high in October.
sections.differing: Reuters, citing a source, says internal email is down; an Equinor spokesperson says it has not lost access to its IT systems, though some applications may be disrupted.
sections.unknown: Attacker identity, intrusion method, scope of compromised systems, whether UK operations are affected, and restoration timeline are not disclosed.

items.headline: France attributes October supermarket fridge sabotage to Iran's IRGC
items.summary: France's cyber agency CERT-FR and Paris prosecutors attribute the October sabotage of refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites to IRGC-linked units. Iran denies it.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Attack acknowledged by French authorities; attribution is a government claim, Iran denies
items.firstReported: 9 November 2026 (CERT-FR report CERTFR-2026-CTI-009, first version); media coverage 9–10 November, UK time

sections.happened: On the night of 11–12 October 2026, attackers remotely accessed refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites and switched on defrost cycles, raising temperatures. Produce was lost and at least 15 fires were reported. On 9 November France formally attributed the attacks to Shahid Kaveh and Shahid Shoostari, IRGC cyber units. Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation.
sections.technical: Attackers remotely connected to refrigeration controllers and changed defrost settings. CERT-FR cites Farsi traces and infrastructure matching other attacks it links to the same units since at least 2020. The report page lists no IOCs or vulnerability.
sections.guidance: The joint US advisory, as reported by TechCrunch and TechTimes, recommends removing controllers from the public internet, changing default passwords, applying updates and isolating operational technology from business networks.
sections.differing: Iran rejects the accusation as baseless. Schneier on Security reports US officials assess Iran responsible with low confidence, linking it to Iran generally, not the IRGC. Pro-Russian groups claimed a separate November wave, unverified.
sections.unknown: Attribution evidence is not published in full; no court finding exists. Other European freezer attacks remain under investigation without official Iran links.

items.headline: N-able cloud server breach disrupts Mail Assure and SpamExperts management
items.summary: Email security provider N-able says unknown actors accessed a server in its hosted cloud, disabling management portal, APIs and quarantine across three regions. Mail flow continues; no customer data loss is evidenced yet.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM
items.labelBasis: Vendor status page and statements; no attacker, method or root cause disclosed. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 19 Nov 2026 (Wednesday), N-able disclosure, reported by The Hacker News; disruption first noticed 16 Nov 2026

sections.happened: N-able investigated a service disruption to Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud from 16 November, then determined it was a security incident. Unknown actors accessed one server, which disabled management interfaces and APIs. Americas, APAC and Europe services remain impacted. Mail flow and filtering continue; restoration is underway.
sections.technical: Unauthorised access to one server in the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. Portal UI, APIs, quarantine and logging remain offline pending security validation. No CVE, ATT&CK technique or intrusion method published.
sections.guidance: N-able says it has contacted partners directly with information on whether action is required for their environment.
sections.differing: N-able first attributed the disruption to platform configuration and service dependencies, later determined it was a security incident. The Hacker News reports it is unrelated to N-central 'Able2Shell' flaws.
sections.unknown: Initial access method, attacker identity, when access began, whether any tenant mail or credentials were exposed, and date of full restoration are not disclosed.

items.headline: Google reports Russian Star Blizzard (COLD RELIC) cloud identity intrusions at two US organisations
items.summary: Google says Russian-linked Star Blizzard, tracked as COLD RELIC, used stolen cloud admin access and MFA fatigue to bulk-download data, then chained into a second US firm.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.labelBasis: Google Threat Intelligence Group report; victims unnamed and the primary blog could not be fetched. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 17 November 2026 (Google blog date); coverage 18-19 November 2026; UK time not stated

sections.happened: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a case study on Russian-linked COLD RELIC (Star Blizzard) and two intrusions at US organisations, in late 2025 and 2026. Google says the group remains active, with phishing seen in November 2026.
sections.technical: Super Admin credentials plus MFA push fatigue via a US residential proxy; full Drive download, Google Takeout export and Alert Center notifications deleted. In 2026, Entra ID credentials and tokens phished via messaging app; rogue MFA device registered.
sections.guidance: Google recommends phishing-resistant MFA such as hardware keys, restricting passkey registration, cloud DLP, proxy/VPN reputation in conditional access, and revoking all sessions on intrusion.
sections.differing: Google cites a US DOJ assessment placing the group within Russia's FSB; no new government statement on these two intrusions was found in the sources read.
sections.unknown: Victim organisations are unnamed; affected account counts and data volumes are not given. Whether UK organisations were targeted is not stated in the sources read.

items.headline: European Commission confirms AI-assisted cyberattack that took staff systems offline
items.summary: The Commission confirmed on 19 November an AI-assisted attack, detected 22 October, that took several applications offline, including HR systems. Politico reported the ARTEX tool was used. No evidence of a staff data breach yet; investigation continues.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Commission spokesperson confirmed incident and AI tool use at press briefing.
items.firstReported: 19 November 2026, Politico (per The Register, Infosecurity Magazine); Commission confirmed same day

sections.happened: Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on 19 November that intrusion was detected on 22 October and confirmed as a cyber-attack on 26 October. Several applications were temporarily taken down as a precaution; most have been restored. Politico reported affected systems included Sysper (HR) and MyPMO (medical reimbursements), with translation services also disrupted for over 10 days. The Commission says it found no evidence of a data breach affecting staff and knows of no ransom demand. The EDPS was notified.
sections.technical: Regnier said the attack was AI-generated using a publicly available tool. Politico, via sources, said CERT-EU identified ARTEX, an open-source LLM-driven penetration-testing framework. CERT-EU's 5 November advisory said activity against its constituency 'highly likely' involved ARTEX and lists T1595, T1588.002 and T1190. The FBI reported over 1,600 exposed ARTEX consoles and some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours. The vector against the Commission is unpublished.
sections.guidance: CERT-EU's ARTEX advisory recommends limiting internet exposure, isolating management panels, emergency patching of exposed assets, monitoring privileged accounts, enabling MFA, hunting for ARTEX artefacts, using EDR and WAFs.
sections.differing: The ARTEX attribution comes from Politico's sources; the Commission confirmed only a 'publicly available' AI tool and did not name it. Politico reported possible staff data exposure; the Commission cites no evidence of a breach.
sections.unknown: Perpetrator, motive, initial access vector, whether any data was accessed, and which applications remain offline are undisclosed. Investigation is ongoing.

items.headline: AttackIQ report maps Iranian groups passing network access to destructive operators
items.summary: AttackIQ's vendor research maps 20 Iranian state-linked groups and describes intrusions where espionage actors handed access to destructive operators. No new incident is disclosed.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM
items.labelBasis: Vendor research release; case details thin, no government or independent confirmation. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 18 November 2026, 10:21 UK time (CIO Influence republication of Business Wire release)

sections.happened: On 18 November 2026 AttackIQ published research mapping 20 Iranian adversaries and their links to government institutions and contractors. It describes two cases where espionage groups handed compromised network access to destructive operators. The report consolidates earlier public reporting; it discloses no new victims.
sections.technical: Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore) handed access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore). Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) passed access to Storm-1084. The report cites 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file and 2,300 network indicators. No CVEs are named in the release.
sections.guidance: AttackIQ says it will release adversary emulations based on documented Iranian TTPs over the coming weeks, so defenders can test detection gaps.
sections.differing: Dark Reading's coverage could not be read (HTTP 403). Group relationships are AttackIQ's own analysis; vendors track the same groups under different names, so mappings are not independently verified.
sections.unknown: Victims and dates behind the handoff cases are not given. AttackIQ says CIRTs and intelligence community members gave input, unnamed. No government confirmation was found.

items.headline: Rakuten Securities says test-environment breach may expose up to 15.72 million accounts
items.summary: Rakuten Securities said unauthorised access on 11 November may have leaked data from a test system holding real customer data: 4.47 million accounts with personal and financial details, 11.25 million with login IDs only. It reports no password leak or unauthorised logins.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Company announcement, reported by Japan Times, Infosecurity and ASCII.jp. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 17 November 2026 (company announcement), reported by Infosecurity Magazine and Japan Times

sections.happened: Rakuten Securities, the online brokerage of Rakuten Group, announced on 17 November that it detected unauthorised access on 16 November and blocked it. Investigation found data in a test environment may have been leaked externally on 11 November. Up to 15.72 million accounts, including former customers, are potentially affected. About 4.47 million include names, birth dates, addresses, contact details, employer, withdrawal bank details, income and asset data; about 11.25 million include only branch/customer codes and login IDs, with no overlap between groups. The company postponed a Shibuya store opening and waived fund-transfer fees.
sections.technical: The test environment normally uses dummy data, but an internal system update required verification with production data, and the access occurred while real customer data was present, according to a company spokesperson quoted by ASCII.jp. The entry vector, attacker and tooling have not been disclosed. The company said it has not confirmed leaks of passwords or transaction PINs.
sections.guidance: Rakuten Securities is notifying affected customers individually and warns of phishing calls and emails impersonating the firm. It said over 90% of customers already use passkeys and urged the rest to adopt them.
sections.differing: Infosecurity Magazine cites 'nearly 16 million' people; the company figure is a maximum of 15.72 million accounts, which may include former customers, not individuals.
sections.unknown: Entry method, attacker identity, whether data was actually exfiltrated, and the cause remain under investigation by the company.

items.headline: TfL Oyster photocard site compromised; about 265,000 customers' account details may be exposed
items.summary: TfL took its Oyster photocard website offline after unauthorised emails were sent from its systems on 16 November. It says about 265,000 customers' account details may be compromised, not passwords or payment data. The ICO has been told; cause undisclosed.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: TfL's director statement quoted by multiple outlets; ICO notified. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 16 November 2026 (TfL became aware); public reporting 18–19 November 2026, e.g. The Register 19 Nov 11:01 UTC

sections.happened: On 16 November 2026 TfL became aware that Oyster photocard customers were receiving emails, sent from TfL's own systems, asking them to create accounts they already had. TfL took the photocard website offline. It now believes about 265,000 customers may have had account details compromised, says the incident is contained, has contacted those affected and informed the ICO. Affected card types include Zip Oyster, 18+ Student, Care Leaver, 60+, Apprentice and Veterans. The site remained offline on 19 November.
sections.technical: TfL has not disclosed how the attackers gained access. The unauthorised emails were generated by TfL's system as a result of the compromise. Per ianVisits, exposed data includes names, addresses, email, phone numbers, dates of birth and security questions and answers; TfL's assessment is that passwords, payment details, journey history, photos and children's Zip card names and birth dates were not accessed.
sections.guidance: TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer, and to change passwords on other services using the same information. Cards still work for travel; renewals and journey history queries go via TfL customer services.
sections.differing: Reports list exposed fields differently: Infosecurity and The Register state only what was not accessed, while ianVisits lists names, contact details, birth dates and security answers. The Register says nothing suggests a link to the 2024 attack.
sections.unknown: Attack vector, actor, how long access lasted, exact data fields, and when the website will return are undisclosed.

items.headline: Wellington IT breach exposes saved payee data at about 40 Irish credit unions
items.summary: Belfast-based supplier Wellington IT says its CU Online platform was hit in an October incident. About 40 Irish credit unions report exposure of members' saved payee details, not login credentials.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Credit unions, the Irish minister and Wellington IT's CEO acknowledge it; total affected unknown. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 17 Nov 2026, 17:20 UK time, TheJournal.ie (earliest in sources); The Register 19 Nov 11:45 UK

sections.happened: An attack on Wellington IT, a Belfast supplier of software and cloud services to credit unions, took place 2 to 4 October 2026. Affected credit unions were told only in recent days. About 40 Irish credit unions report exposure of saved payee records. Minister Robert Troy called the delay 'not acceptable'. Total affected individuals is unknown.
sections.technical: Notices seen by the Irish Examiner say an automated script made five million requests to exploit an authorisation flaw, using valid credentials to access private records. The flaw was reportedly closed 6 October. No activity logs to show which member data was taken.
sections.guidance: St Canice's Credit Union advised members to stay alert to phishing and impersonation, and not to move money because anyone claims it must be made safe.
sections.differing: Wellington IT says it notified customers once the risk was confirmed; Minister Troy says the breach occurred in October and credit unions learned of it only in recent days.
sections.unknown: Total number of individuals affected, exact data fields per institution, whether other Wellington IT clients are involved, and attacker identity remain undisclosed.

items.headline: Gentlemen ransomware group lists Nvidia on leak site; Nvidia cites possible third-party incident
items.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware group listed Nvidia on its leak site with a 28 November countdown but no proof. Nvidia says it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner and has found no sign its own systems were affected.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM
items.labelBasis: Group claim without proof; Nvidia denies own systems affected.
items.firstReported: 19 Nov 2026, BleepingComputer (page shows 04:23, time zone not stated)

sections.happened: The Gentlemen ransomware group added Nvidia to its dark web leak site, with a countdown ending 28 November. According to SecurityWeek, the listing has a logo and a generic company description, and says details of stolen data will follow. iThome reports a Tox contact for negotiation and no sample data or intrusion date. Nvidia told BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner and found no indication its systems or networks were affected.
sections.technical: No technical details of an Nvidia intrusion have been published. The Gentlemen emerged around mid-2025, became a ransomware-as-a-service operation offering affiliates up to 90% of proceeds (BleepingComputer), and uses double extortion. Microsoft tracks its operators as Storm-2697 (SecurityWeek). Sophos reports affiliates used compromised credentials and legitimate administrative tools, with ransomware deployed within 24 hours in one case. The leak site lists over 1,100 claimed victims.
sections.differing: The group implies it holds Nvidia data; Nvidia says it has no indication its own systems were affected. No evidence has been published, so the company's account is currently better supported.
sections.unknown: Whether any data was stolen, the identity of the third-party partner, what data it holds, and whether the listing relates to that incident.

items.headline: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI package compromised with credential stealer
items.summary: Malicious agent-framework releases 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were published to PyPI on 17 November 2026. They run a credential stealer at Python startup and send data to a webhook.site endpoint. PyPI quarantined both.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Multiple security firms document the malicious versions; PyPI quarantined them.
items.firstReported: 17 Nov 2026 (PyPI publication); first public reports 18 Nov 2026 (BleepingComputer, Socket, StepSecurity); UK time not stated

sections.happened: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft's agent-framework package were published on PyPI on 17 November 2026. Both kept a dependency on legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0. PyPI quarantined the first release; a second was published about 2.5 minutes later and quarantined about eight minutes after that. Roughly 200,000 monthly PyPI downloads.
sections.technical: 1.26.1 runs a stealer via agent_framework_meta.pth at Python startup, harvesting cloud and developer secrets and Azure managed identity tokens. 1.26.2 adds GitHub Actions OIDC token requests. Both exfiltrate to a webhook.site URL.
sections.guidance: BleepingComputer advises rebuilding from a clean environment on the safe 1.26.0 release and rotating any credentials exposed to the compromised environment.
sections.differing: Reporting does not say how publishing access was obtained; BleepingComputer says Microsoft had not responded by publication. Socket, StepSecurity and Ox describe the same versions.
sections.unknown: How the attacker obtained PyPI publishing access, whether Microsoft-owned credentials were used, the attacker's identity, and install counts of the malicious versions are not public.

items.headline: F5 patches five critical NGINX flaws ('NGINX2Root'); public PoC exists for HTTP/2 bug CVE-2026-123007
items.summary: F5 fixed five critical NGINX bugs, including two HTTP/2 flaws enabling unauthenticated remote code execution. Rapid7 and Censys published proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007. F5 and Xint report no in-the-wild exploitation; exposure depends on configuration.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: F5 advisory, Rapid7 write-up and multiple outlets agree; PoCs public.
items.firstReported: 18 Nov 2026, Infosecurity Magazine (Wiz, Xint, Rapid7 and others disclosed same day)

sections.happened: On 18 November 2026 F5 released fixes for five critical NGINX flaws (CVSS 4.0 9.2) found independently by Wiz, Xint, Rapid7, Ikotas Labs and Metnir. Xint names the set NGINX2Root. Fixes are in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1. Rapid7 and Censys published PoC code for CVE-2026-123007. Censys counted about 8.8 million potentially exposed services, plus about 104 million not disclosing versions.
sections.technical: CVE-2026-123007 (CWE-191 integer underflow) is in HTTP/2 flow control; affected since 1.9.5. A client cancels queued response data, so nginx copies a later response with an invalid length, corrupting heap memory. CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free in HTTP/2 proxying (1.19.7 to 1.31.8). The others are use-after-frees in HTTP/3 proxying (CVE-2026-121810), resolver subrequests (CVE-2026-123634) and mail proxy (CVE-2026-113425). Rapid7's RCE needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data and an x86-64 glibc AVX-512 memcpy path. F5 says code execution requires ASLR disabled or bypassed.
sections.guidance: F5 lists NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 (NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1, 37.3.0.1) as fixed releases. Wiz and Infosecurity Magazine report that disabling HTTP/2 is the stopgap until patching; BleepingComputer notes it covers only the two HTTP/2 flaws.
sections.differing: Xint said 98.9% of version-disclosing hosts were in the affected range; Florian Roth said exposure claims based on version alone mislead, as exploitation needs HTTP/2 and non-default setups. Censys reproduced the bug without Rapid7's large traffic volume.
sections.unknown: No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. Real exposure after backported fixes, and how many of the undisclosed-version hosts are vulnerable, is unknown.

items.headline: ICJ finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya in 2017 operations
items.summary: On 19 November 2026 the International Court of Justice ruled, in The Gambia v. Myanmar, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State in 2017. The judgment is final and binding; Myanmar has long denied the allegations.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: ICJ press release and Reuters report the judgment.
items.firstReported: 19 November 2026, around 10:00 Hague time (09:00 UK): ICJ judgment; Reuters reported during the reading

sections.happened: The ICJ delivered its merits judgment in the case The Gambia brought in November 2019 on behalf of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It found Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the 2017 'clearance operations'. It also found Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by individuals acting alongside its forces, to punish it, and to enact legislation, but did not find direct and public incitement. Reuters reported findings that security forces killed thousands of civilians and committed widespread sexual violence. The genocide finding was carried 9 votes to 6 by the judges named in the operative clause.
sections.differing: Reuters describes it as the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide; The Jerusalem Post says 10,000 Rohingya were killed, a figure not confirmed in the ICJ material read. Myanmar has consistently rejected the accusations, citing attacks by armed militia.
sections.unknown: Reparations, Myanmar's response and enforcement are not stated in the sources read. Full reasoning and dissents were not read beyond the press release extract.

items.headline: Ukraine and FBI arrest four suspected ransomware gang members
items.summary: Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, arrested four suspected members of a ransomware extortion group linked to at least $40.5 million in payments from 28 companies.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM
items.labelBasis: Ukrainian authorities publicly announced the arrests; payment figures are official claims not independently verified. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: Wednesday 18 November 2026, Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office statement via The Record; UK time not stated

sections.happened: Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office and National Police, with the FBI, ran 66 searches in Kyiv and 11 regions and detained four suspected key members of a group of at least 27 people. Authorities say at least 28 companies paid over $40.5 million.
sections.technical: Attackers impersonated IT support, used AI-generated voice messages in calls, and sent phishing pages mimicking corporate VPNs; victims were pushed to install TeamViewer or AnyDesk. Court records name Chaos ransomware.
sections.differing: Reports link the wider network to former Conti members, but authorities have not confirmed individual affiliations with Conti, BlackSuit or Chaos.
sections.unknown: Total damage (authorities say it may be higher), arrest locations, suspect names and the full group structure are not disclosed. Several victims' own disclosures did not confirm payments.

items.headline: UK tribunal rules Home Office must confirm it issued Apple a technical capability notice
items.summary: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on 19 November 2026 that the Home Office has not shown that confirming a technical capability notice to Apple would harm national security. Hearings on the substance and on what details can be released are expected next year.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Tribunal ruling reported by Reuters, TechCrunch and claimant Privacy International. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: 19 November 2026, Privacy International and TechCrunch (07:32 PST); Reuters 16:11 Israel time via Jerusalem Post

sections.happened: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on 19 November 2026 that the Home Office had not established that confirming it gave Apple a technical capability notice (TCN) would damage national security. The government had relied on its 'neither confirm nor deny' policy. The tribunal cited public disclosures, including press reports apparently from government briefings. Privacy International and Liberty brought the claim; Apple has a separate pending claim, filed July 2026. Liberty called it the first known compelled confirmation of a secret technical order.
sections.unknown: Notice contents, scope and what details may be released are undecided. Private judgments remain undisclosed. The Home Office and Apple had not commented. The judgment text itself was not read.
sections.differing: The government argued confirmation would give material assistance to hostile actors. The tribunal found it had not shown damage. Reuters dates the first notice to January 2025; Privacy International says it was reported in February 2025.
sections.guidance: Apple has previously said it has never built a backdoor or master key and never will. Under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, recipients of a TCN are legally barred from commenting on it publicly.

sections.happened: Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, was sentenced to 72 months in US federal prison, the fifth and final defendant sentenced. Prosecutors say the group hacked at least a dozen companies and stole over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individuals.

items.headline: Crimean Bridge struck three times in a week; Putin rules out energy truce and pledges response
items.summary: Ukraine struck the Kerch (Crimean) Bridge on 16–19 November; Reuters-verified imagery shows the road arch collapsed. Putin then said no energy or sea truce would be negotiated and promised a 'more painful' response and rebuilding.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Russian ministry, Ukrainian General Staff and Reuters-verified imagery agree on damage.
items.firstReported: 19 Nov 2026, Reuters via The Moscow Times (Ukrinform timeline dates first strike to 16 Nov)

sections.happened: Ukraine attacked the 19 km Kerch Strait bridge on 16 November, again on 17 November and overnight on 19 November. Reuters reported verified images showing the central road section destroyed on Tuesday. Russia's transport ministry said a drone attack suspended rail services, with no injuries; Crimea's governor said trains would resume about 16:00 local time. Ukraine's General Staff said Neptune missiles damaged the railway track. Speaking in China after talks with Xi and Trump, Putin said there would be no energy or sea truce, Russia would respond more painfully, and the bridge would be rebuilt.
sections.differing: Ukraine's General Staff calls the bridge a main military supply route; Putin called it a civilian facility and said military and fuel cargo had stopped long ago. Reuters says the army now relies more on the land corridor. Putin said rail was restored; Russia's ministry reported a suspension.
sections.unknown: Extent of road-span and rail damage, rebuild timeline, the form and timing of Russia's promised response, and whether any truce talks continue are unconfirmed.

items.headline: Houthi missile damages PIF Tower in Riyadh's financial district
items.summary: A suspected Houthi missile struck Riyadh's PIF Tower, Saudi sovereign wealth fund headquarters, before dawn on 19 November, per Reuters sources. The coalition cited debris damage. No casualties were reported initially. The Houthis had earlier claimed missile attacks on Riyadh's airport and a financial centre.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Coalition acknowledged damage; Reuters, AFP and Semafor report the tower hit. Primary source not read; based on secondary reporting.
items.firstReported: Before dawn 19 Nov 2026 Riyadh time (early UK morning); Reuters, via The National (updated 07:04 UTC)

sections.happened: Before dawn on 19 November 2026 a loud blast was heard in Riyadh after a civil defence alert. Reuters, citing three sources, reported that PIF Tower, headquarters of the Public Investment Fund in King Abdullah Financial District, was hit by a Houthi missile; windows were blown out across seven to eight floors. The coalition said it had dealt with a missile threat and that debris caused material damage. A Houthi statement on Wednesday claimed cruise missile attacks on King Khalid airport and a financial centre. Aramco's building in the district was hit on 8 November.
sections.unknown: Casualty figures, the exact missile type, whether it was intercepted, and any Houthi claim for the PIF Tower strike are not reported. Operational impact on the airport is unconfirmed.
sections.differing: The coalition attributes damage to falling debris and did not say whether the missile was intercepted; Reuters sources say the tower was struck by an incoming missile. Houthi claims come via Xinhua/CGTN (Chinese state media) and were unverified.
sections.guidance: No official guidance for residents beyond the Saudi Civil Defence aerial threat alert and all-clear was reported in the sources read.

items.headline: Echo study finds three frontier AI models barely agree on code flaws
items.summary: Echo tested Claude Mythos 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3 on the same open-source code. Of 121 issues, one was found by all three; most findings were unvalidated.
items.label: VENDOR-ACKNOWLEDGED
items.labelBasis: Vendor research release; projects unnamed, findings not maintainer-confirmed
items.firstReported: 18 November 2026, 08:00 UTC (08:00 UK time), Echo press release via GlobeNewswire

sections.happened: On 18 November 2026 Echo published a controlled comparison: three AI models hunted vulnerabilities in two Maven libraries and one npm package. Of 121 distinct potential issues, one was found by all three models and 83% by a single model. Projects remain unnamed pending maintainer notification.
sections.technical: Nine runs produced 446 findings, cut to 152, with 55 High or Critical sent to automated proof-of-concept testing; Echo reports 31 confirmed at High. Costs: about $303 (Claude Mythos), $30 (GPT-5.6 Sol), $22 (GLM-5.3) for hunts.
sections.guidance: None published beyond Echo's note that automated validation is not maintainer confirmation and that the work is a controlled comparison, not a benchmark.
sections.differing: Infosecurity reports 42 findings passed automated testing; Echo says these may not be distinct bugs. Nature quotes UCL researcher Steven Murdoch: AI-found Java flaw 'not one of the top ten vulnerabilities this year'.
sections.unknown: Projects, CVEs and maintainer responses are unpublished. Each model ran once. Nature's Murdoch says recent outages were probably unrelated to AI-driven attacks; TechCrunch reports Palmer Luckey saying otherwise.

items.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth as science and engineering data stop
items.summary: Voyager 1 passed one light-day (about 25.9 billion km) from Earth on 18 November 2026. Since 14 November only a carrier signal has been received, with no science or engineering data. NASA is investigating, possibly linked to an October 48-hour contact loss.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: NASA mission blog states both the data loss and the milestone.
items.firstReported: 18 Nov 2026 (evening US time; NASA Science Voyager blog)

sections.happened: On 14 November 2026 the Voyager 1 team found the spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data after a Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra locked onto its carrier signal but received no data. NASA says the probe reached one light-day from Earth on 18 November, roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km), confirmed on 19 November from the carrier signal and trajectory models. Engineers are determining the cause.
sections.technical: NASA says the carrier signal shows the Attitude and Articulation Control computer is keeping the antenna pointed at Earth and the transmitter works. It suggests the fault lies in the onboard computer that collects data from subsystems and formats it for transmission. A similar 2023 no-data fault was traced to an onboard computer.
sections.guidance: NASA states engineers are working to determine the cause and next steps, and that diagnosis may take weeks or longer because signals need 24 hours each way.
sections.differing: The Register says the October interruption could have followed safe mode after a thruster failover; the NASA blog page read does not state a cause. NASA says only that it is checking for a connection.
sections.unknown: The cause, whether it is linked to the October 48-hour contact loss, and when data will return are all unknown.

items.headline: NIH director asks Nature Medicine to probe authorship of 2020 COVID origin paper
items.summary: NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya wrote to Nature Medicine seeking an investigation into the authorship of its 2020 ‘proximal origin’ paper on SARS-CoV-2; one author rejects the claims.
items.label: UNCONFIRMED CLAIM
items.labelBasis: Rests on a single outlet (Science); the letter itself was not read.
items.firstReported: About 18 Nov 2026, Science (exact date and UK time not confirmed)

sections.happened: NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya sent a letter to the editor of Nature Medicine requesting an investigation into the authorship of ‘The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2’, published 17 March 2020. Science reports he asks the journal to consider retracting it over concerns it was ghostwritten by former NIH officials.
sections.differing: Bhattacharya cites ghostwriting concerns. Author Ian Lipkin says the author list reflects who conceived, drafted and revised the paper and that it was ‘definitely not ghostwritten’.
sections.unknown: Nature Medicine’s response and any retraction decision. The cluster’s NIH funding-bill story could not be read and is not covered here.

sources.title: Science: NIH director calls for new probe of controversial COVID-19 origin paper

items.headline: UKRI funds 80+ proof-of-concept projects; STFC Central Laser Facility joins First Light Fusion work
items.summary: UKRI reported over 80 translation proof-of-concept projects with £16.8m committed, and STFC’s Central Laser Facility began fast-ignition modelling with First Light Fusion.
items.label: CONFIRMED
items.labelBasis: Primary UKRI news releases dated 18 November 2026 state the funding and partnership.
items.firstReported: 18 Nov 2026, UKRI news release (time not stated)

sections.happened: On 18 November 2026 UKRI announced over 80 translation proof-of-concept projects funded with Defra, with £16.8 million committed; the headline says £15 million. Separately, STFC’s Central Laser Facility began work with First Light Fusion on fast-ignition modelling for its FLARE inertial fusion concept.
sections.differing: The release headline says £15 million; the body says £16.8 million has been committed. The release does not reconcile the two figures.
sections.unknown: Individual award values and total programme size are not stated; CLF modelling results and timing of any integrated FLARE experiment are not given.
